name: Processor

claims.claim_text: If a fifty-cent microcontroller can do the job, use it. The boundary is sharp and worth knowing: watching three lines toggling at ten megahertz and extracting a bit pattern on the fly is beyond any processor on the market, and that is where programmable logic earns its cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you have to watch three signal lines that are toggling at 10 megahertz
claims.speaker: Philip Frieden
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: A processor has to stop and crunch the data, which makes its timing non-deterministic; programmable logic streams data through as it arrives. Where the requirement is that the timing be exactly right rather than merely fast, that difference decides the architecture.
claims.quote_verbatim: using processors, using, using FPGAs and FPGAs, you're streaming the data through
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Greg Charvat Returns With A Book! - Laboratory Literature Laureate

claims.claim_text: Switch debouncing belongs in hardware. Handing the problem to firmware spends processor time and attention permanently to compensate for a component that a capacitor would have fixed once.
claims.quote_verbatim: processor has better things to do than to fix your stupid broken hardware
claims.speaker: Elecia White
claims.episode_title: Is This A Show?

claims.claim_text: Programmable logic vendors putting hard processors back into their devices was a concession rather than an advance: soft processors were not what customers wanted, and the industry response was to commit the function to fixed silicon.
claims.quote_verbatim: People want processors
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Solar, FPGAs and Maxim Integrated - Solar Shopper Sickness

claims.claim_text: Engineers stay with processors they already know because a working board support package or a default project that builds is worth more than a cheaper part. Paying ten dollars more per chip to avoid starting from nothing is a rational trade, and it is how most part selection actually happens.
claims.quote_verbatim: pay 10 bucks for a chip just to not have to start at the beginning again
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Contextual Electronics, ClubJameco and Solderpaste - Lifelong Learning Likelihood

claims.claim_text: Changing processor means retargeting the software and forfeiting the accumulated polish that went into the existing stack. The component saving has to exceed that lost work, which is why cost-reduction exercises so often stop at the processor.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you switch processors, then you switch your entire software stack
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Three Hundred Down, Three Hundred To Go

claims.claim_text: The claim that choosing a common architecture lets you move between vendors seamlessly does not survive contact with a real design. The instruction set ports; the peripherals, the register maps and the tooling do not.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you choose Arm as your processor, then you can just move to any vendor seamlessly
claims.episode_title: eReaders, datasheets & board assembly - Yearly Yeasty Yapping

claims.claim_text: Discovering at the third prototype that the firmware will not fit the chosen processor is a late and expensive failure, and the proposal that follows is usually to drop a feature and revisit the processor in a later revision — which in practice means the feature never arrives.
claims.quote_verbatim: the processor we've put in this thing, we can't fit everything in
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Gotta Update My Dog

claims.claim_text: Before accepting that a processor change means rewriting the software, check for a pin-compatible member of the same family with the same tools. Large families exist precisely so that a capacity problem can be answered with a different part number rather than a redesign.
claims.quote_verbatim: another family that's pin compatible and, you know, the tools are the same
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Gotta Update My Dog

claims.claim_text: Product line refreshes routinely arrive as an obsolescence emergency: the assumption that the processor will remain available holds until it does not, and by then the redesign is unplanned and urgent.
claims.quote_verbatim: oh, crap, we can't buy the processor anymore
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An interview with Alvaro and Jen from the URE Podcast

claims.claim_text: Being application-oriented rather than processor-oriented is a defensible stance for an embedded engineer: the processor is a means to an end, and the interesting constraints usually live in the application rather than in the part.
claims.quote_verbatim: are a tool to get from here to there
claims.speaker: Elecia White
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Elecia White - Wirewove Worshipping Wookieist?

claims.claim_text: The wish for a single obvious processor choice is real and unattainable, because the range of applications is effectively unbounded and every one of them justifies another variant. Selection is therefore a recurring cost of the discipline rather than a problem to be solved once.
claims.quote_verbatim: want there to be just one choice so I don't have to make it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Elecia White - Wirewove Worshipping Wookieist?

claims.claim_text: Useful processing happens at sub-microwatt power levels — a part clocking at thirty-two kilohertz still moves data around usefully. What has enabled new applications is not raw speed but the collapse in the power required to do modest work.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can do useful processing in, you know, sub micro watt levels
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Driscoll - Impacable Interdisciplinary Inventor

claims.claim_text: Faster processors are not what unlocks new functionality; shrinking the size and the power is. That reframing is what makes energy harvesting — even from static charge — worth pursuing, because the target it has to reach keeps coming down.
claims.quote_verbatim: processors are getting faster, but that's not what
claims.speaker: Scott Driscoll
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Driscoll - Impacable Interdisciplinary Inventor

claims.claim_text: Integrating touch sensing, security and similar continuous functions into a companion chip means the main processor never has to wake for them. Battery life improves out of proportion to the function moved, because the cost avoided is the wake-up rather than the work.
claims.quote_verbatim: don't have to wake up your main huge big gulping processor
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Be Tidy

claims.claim_text: Where a design carries two processors, letting each put the other to sleep gives the power management to whichever one has the relevant information — the radio module knowing there is nothing to send, or the application knowing the user has finished.
claims.quote_verbatim: both kind of processors, the module and the AppMega can put each other to sleep
claims.speaker: Colin
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Colin Karpfinger - Blendling Bean Brio

claims.claim_text: Large memory in a mobile-class part comes from stacking the memory die physically on top of the processor die inside one package. It is why such a device offers far more RAM than its pin count suggests and why the memory is not separately sourceable.
claims.quote_verbatim: got the DRAM, the silicon. It's physically piggybacked on top of the silicon of the processor
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jack Ganssle - Embedded Elchee Epexegesis

claims.claim_text: An application processor and a bare processor are different products: one arrives with display drivers, memory and peripherals integrated and is nearly a system, while the other requires everything to be built around it before it does anything useful.
claims.quote_verbatim: OMAP has everything in it. It's got display drivers and the whole works
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Multicopter, DIY drones & Tektronix - Zappy Zendik Zoilism

claims.claim_text: Putting a microcontroller and an application processor on the same board gives both real-time behaviour and a general-purpose operating system with a graphical interface — the combination that neither a small development board nor a single-board computer provides alone.
claims.quote_verbatim: try to combine the microcontroller and processor
claims.speaker: Robert Feranec
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Robert Feranec

claims.claim_text: Embedding a small processor inside a custom chip to handle low-speed state during idle periods keeps the design from hard-coding behaviour into silicon, which is what preserves the ability to change the product after tape-out.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's actually all processor-driven in there
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Absorptive Augmented Actuality

claims.claim_text: Vision is where the demand for processing power genuinely lives: even on the fastest available boards, real-time vision work was limited to something like 640 by 480 at fifteen frames per second, which is what makes the question of what all that performance is for concrete.
claims.quote_verbatim: you still can only do, like, you know, 640 by 480 at 15 frames per second
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Richardson - Raspberry Risorgimento Regent

claims.claim_text: Whatever happens to fabrication cost, processors will remain too complex to produce outside industrial facilities. Predictions of home chip manufacture consistently underestimate how much of the difficulty is complexity rather than equipment cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: there is no effing way in hell that you're going to print these things and build your chips in your own home
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Freescale, Hackerspaces, Printable Electronics - Publish Popular Parts Please!

claims.claim_text: Building a processor is comparatively simple; building the compilers, debuggers and libraries around it is the hard part. That asymmetry is what makes an established instruction set so valuable to its owner — the tools were built by a community, and the architecture's licence is what prevents anyone reusing them.
claims.quote_verbatim: building a processor is actually very, very simple. The hard part usually is not building the processor
claims.speaker: Claire Wolf
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Claire (née 'Clifford') Wolf

claims.claim_text: Several enabling conditions arrived at once — adequate battery life, very cheap processors and reasonably mature software — and it is their coincidence rather than any single advance that moved connected devices from demonstration to product.
claims.quote_verbatim: battery life's good enough. Processors are super cheap
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Amazon Moves In, Dave Says Run

claims.claim_text: A processor changing operating mode changes the current drawn from the supply, and that step translates into conducted emissions. A compliance failure can therefore originate in firmware behaviour that no schematic review would flag.
claims.quote_verbatim: your processor could be switching into a different mode that causes, you know, increased current
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Chris Becomes Self Employed - Quixotic Quitting Quaere

claims.claim_text: Adding compiled code to an on-device interpreted environment invokes the standard compiler against the whole firmware, so the toolchain has to know the target processor. Inline assembly is handled separately by a small purpose-built translator rather than by the full compiler.
claims.quote_verbatim: it needs to know what processor is there
claims.speaker: Tony DiCola
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tony DiCola

attribution_notes: attribution_reliable was not trusted. ep103 (Philip Freidin), ep187 (Elecia White), ep226 (Colin Karpfinger), ep316 (Robert Feranec), ep323 (Tony DiCola) and ep374 (Claire Wolf) label host questions with the guest's name; only material unambiguously the guest's own was used.
ep126 records both hosts under machine speaker labels; the claim about architecture portability carries speaker: null.
ep147 labels Dave Jones's summary of Jeri Ellsworth's design as his own; the claim is kept as his restatement, which is what the passage supports.
Speculation about specific vendor acquisitions and product-line politics was excluded as neither transferable nor durable.
